The vibrations were stronger than they’d been ten minutes ago.
Now they weren’t just coming up through the soles of their feet; they were shaking their whole bodies.
*It’s coming.*
Everyone felt it at once, and realized anew how close they stood to death.
But they couldn’t back down.
They were humanity’s last line of defense.
They must have been given their powers for this very moment.
“Hey, rookie.”
“Yes, Team Leader.”
The young man answered hoarsely when the call came from behind him.
At some point, his hand and his Tower Shield had stopped shaking.
“Thanks.”
“What?”
“For saying I’m someone’s dream.
Thanks.”
Still smiling, the middle-aged man—Im Kkeokjeong, Team Leader of Ares Guild’s Team 32—pulled his helmet down low.
*I may not be able to become like that guy, but I’m a Hunter, too.*
He fixed his gaze on the dust cloud rising a few hundred meters away and shouted with all his might.
“Formation—!”
At that moment, as a roar pierced the sky, the communicator on Im Kkeokjeong’s chest received a message.
—Attention, all Hunters.
Alpha—Alpha has awakened.
A blade-sharp wind swept across the battlefield.

chapters.title: Chapter 1174
paragraphs: The first thought I had when I opened my eyes was simple.
*Is this a dream?*
It wasn’t an unreasonable thought.
Anyone who saw that spotless white ceiling, dozens of meters overhead in a room the size of a sports field, would probably have thought the same.
But a moment later, I realized it was real.
*This place...*
I recognized it.
Or rather, maybe not familiar exactly, but I’d definitely been here before.
I vividly remembered staying in a similar place, both in that dreamlike realm of my thoughts and in reality.
Then a voice confirmed it.
“You were sleeping soundly.”
His voice carried unmistakable exhaustion.
I turned toward it, saw a familiar face, and parted my dry lips.
“Yeah. I do tend to sleep a lot.”
I saw a faint smile appear on Team Leader Choi’s usually stern face.
From the way he looked at me, I was probably smiling, too.
For Hunters, meeting again alive meant something special.
But the smile that briefly touched Choi Minwoo’s lips, and the joy of seeing each other again, lasted only a moment.
They were alive, as they’d just said. Which meant they had to face reality.
“How long has it been?”
Jin Taekyung didn’t beat around the bush, and Choi Minwoo saw no reason to hide the truth.
“Three days. About seventy-six hours, to be exact.”
“...Three days.”
It wasn’t a long time.
For someone living an ordinary life, it was just the blink of an eye.
But Jin Taekyung knew better.
He’d known from the moment he saw Choi Minwoo, exhausted from head to toe.
No—maybe he’d known even before he lost consciousness.
“A lot happened while you were away, Mr. Jin.”
Choi Minwoo paused to catch his breath, then added, almost to himself,
“A lot. So much.”
For a while, only Choi Minwoo’s voice echoed through the vast, empty white space. When his story ended, the silence that followed lasted even longer.
Unlike Jin Taekyung’s mind, where countless scenes and voices were still swirling together.
*Let me ask you one thing.*
“You have my permission.”
*Why?*
“If you can grow even a little stronger, what comes next will be all the more entertaining.”
Jin Taekyung remembered the end of the wicked Dragon who had made the world tremble.
He remembered the vivid emotion that even the shadow of death looming right in front of him couldn’t hide.
“Fight with every last bit of strength you have. Keep surpassing yourself. Keep struggling.”
Even as his final breath faded, Morgoth hadn’t shown the slightest anger.
“So I can see it from where I am.”
It had been nothing more than a sigh.
A sigh born of regret: he hadn’t been the one chosen by God, and he wouldn’t get to experience the grand game about to begin.
The vague foreboding Jin Taekyung had felt then had become reality three days later, sweeping across the world.
*He knew what was going to happen.*
Judging by Morgoth’s actions, Jin Taekyung didn’t think he’d wanted this outcome from the start.
But that no longer mattered.
The Dragon Heart—Pandora’s box, filled with every kind of calamity—had opened.
Not in myth, but in reality.
The power contained in the wicked Dragon’s heart, which had pulsed for thousands of years, was incomparably greater than that of the Hatchling Michael Silbert had defeated in Paris.
It was without precedent.
Even if Choi Minwoo hadn’t told him what had happened, Jin Taekyung’s own senses would have proved it.
*Beep-beep-beep.*
**System** —There are System messages you haven’t checked. —The distribution and density of magical power are skyrocketing... —Current progress of the rift...
Jin Taekyung wasn’t the only one who’d woken up after three days.
Dozens of holographic windows he hadn’t been able to check while unconscious flooded his vision like a wave, sweeping him along with them.
Among them, his eyes caught on words glowing an especially vivid red, like reefs hidden beneath a violent current.

**System** —Quest success requirements have not been met. —Main Quest, Rift and Collapse, has failed. —A new Main Quest, The Foreordained Collapse, has been created. —Would you like to view this Quest? Y / N
Jin Taekyung thought that final message, asking for his consent, was crueler than ever.
He had no other choice.
*...View Quest.*
And a little while later, Jin Taekyung finally broke the long silence.
“Team Leader Choi.”
“Yes?”
“I need you to gather everyone. Right now.”
Choi Minwoo already had a good idea who Jin Taekyung meant by “everyone.”
He knew the request included one being who was more human than most humans, too.
Maybe it was because the space was so vast, but Team Leader Choi’s absence—he’d left without asking a single question—felt like a big one.
Still, I wasn’t lonely.
I had someone to talk to.
Granted, there was the slight problem that he was in no condition to hold a conversation.
*Knock, knock.*
I tapped on the transparent recovery capsule as if it were a door, then gazed at the face of the man sleeping deeply inside.
*Cheon Taemin.*
I’d learned as soon as I regained consciousness that this was a secret space deep beneath the Pentagon.
A vast hospital room and shelter built for one person alone, inaccessible even to the President of the United States.
“Well, now there are two of us.”
My muttered words received no answer.
As always.
I kept talking anyway.
“I know what kind of person you are. Better than anyone else in the world.”
There was no longer any doubt that Cheon Taemin and the Martial God were the same person.
Or that he’d been a Player who’d used the System before I did.
But one question remained deep in my heart.
“How are you... still alive?”
It was a cruel thing to ask someone who was still breathing, but I had to ask.
The instruction manual for that beat-up old capsule, where all of this had begun, said the capsule remained permanently bound to its Player until the Player died.
Ironically, that incomprehensible error was what had given me the reckless courage to face Morgoth alone.
*I thought that if I died, you might wake up.*
I swallowed the words before they could leave my throat.
At the same time, I remembered something Morgoth had said.
*The one chosen by God.*
I didn’t doubt it anymore.
I had been chosen.
Whether I’d wanted it or not.
Some great being existed—a being humanity had never encountered, even after reaching beyond the clouds and into space. Another dimension existed, too.
And that unknown being was asking me a question.
Through the receiver called the System.
*Open System window. View Quest.*
*Ding!*

**System Quest** The Foreordained Collapse At long last, the balance of the world has crumbled. This is no mere coincidence. It is the spark left behind by an invader from beyond this world, and the flame kindled by all of humanity, yourself included. But one last chance remains. Stave off the collapse, however little you can, and save the world. At the same time, remember this: Just as a mountain leaves its mark when it moves, every choice you make will affect the whole world. **Grade:** None **Restriction:** Jin Taekyung **Mission:** ??? **Reward:** ??? **Failure:** ??? —This Quest may change drastically depending on the Player’s choices. —Be as cautious as you can. A single choice may bring about irreversible consequences.
This was a first.
No Quest had ever warned me in words or a tone so grave.
The decision I’d already made began to waver.
Maybe—maybe my choice really would bring about the terrible consequences the System had warned me about.
But there was no time.

I couldn’t shake the feeling that if I delayed any longer, things would truly become irreversible. It weighed on my body and mind as surely as the hurried footsteps I could sense beyond the countless layers of magic covering this place.
*Whoosh.*
The spells came undone under the Grand Mage’s hand, revealing familiar faces.
Comrades I could trust with my back. Friends I’d gladly give my life for. People I could call family now.
I turned to them and spoke.
“Have any of you ever traveled between dimensions?”
The Skeleton—or rather, the Undead King—muttered uneasily.
“Uh... are you still half asleep?”
“...You little shit.”
Of course it sounded like a dream.
A nightmare, if anything.
The people—or, more precisely, several people and one monster—couldn’t bring themselves to speak even after I’d finished explaining.
The first to break the unspoken standoff was the huge Grand Mage, who’d looked dazed throughout the whole story.
“I’m serious. If you’d said something like that two or three hundred years ago, they’d have called you a witch and burned you at the stake.”
“I agree, but I’m not a woman.”
“By the time they tied you to the stake, you would’ve been. They’d just have to cut off what’s dangling down there.”
“Fair enough.”
“Actually, we don’t have to go that far back. Before the Great Cataclysm, that story would’ve landed you in a psychiatric hospital.”
“Probably.”
“But now... Yeah. This is after that damn Great Cataclysm. And I’m the Grand Mage.”
That was right.
These were the times we lived in.
It had only been three days since we’d fought to take down a Dragon the size of an aircraft carrier. After hearing my whole story, no one suggested putting me in a psychiatric hospital.
Not even the monster.
None of them doubted a word I’d said.
Even if the world were a little different, I was sure they would have believed me.
Just as Jeok Cheongang had believed in me.
And I’d had only one reason to reveal the secret I’d kept deep in my heart.
“I’m... going to leave. To put an end to all of this.”
I knew where the invader from beyond this world was.

chapters.title: Chapter 1175
paragraphs: Every story has an ending.
Jin Taekyung already knew what it would take to end this nightmarish catastrophe. He had to defeat one being.
“Demon King Asmodeus.”
The name was a curse to modern humanity. As it left his lips, the air around them seemed to freeze.
The old heroes, who still remembered that horrific past vividly after all these decades, looked especially stricken.
“...Asmodeus?”
“That—that can’t be.”
Chuck Hagel and Magic Johnson spoke almost at the same time. Their reactions were exactly what Jin Taekyung had expected.
He’d shared his deepest secrets with them, but they couldn’t take it all in so quickly.
No, this was closer to an instinctive defense: the human urge to deny reality rather than live through that nightmare again.
“I understand. I thought the same thing for a long time.”
Jin Taekyung meant every word.
He hadn’t experienced the Great Cataclysm firsthand, but he’d been born on its final day.
Growing up, he’d been taught about it until he was sick of hearing it: what had happened during the Great Cataclysm, and how humanity had survived.
And how the ruler of the Demon Realm who had caused the Great Cataclysm met his end at the hands of a great hero born of humanity, without leaving so much as a trace.
But...
“He’s alive. I’m certain of it. In another world, under the name Lord of Heaven.”
Just as Cheon Taemin had existed as the Martial God, the king of demons had gained a new name in another world.
The beginning and the end of all this.
Jin Taekyung was certain. To reach the end of the path he’d walked—and the path still ahead of him—he had to reach that bastard.
But no one else could see the shape of the enormous puzzle he’d pieced together while traveling between two worlds. They could only trust the young man standing before them.
And someone did.
“I see. Understood.”
Choi Minwoo’s voice was calm. That made it sound all the more unnatural.
As Cheon Taemin’s only direct blood relative, Choi Minwoo had more reason than anyone there to be shaken by what he’d heard.
His gaze passed briefly over the others, then settled on Jin Taekyung. It didn’t waver in the slightest.
“If that’s what you believe, Mr. Jin, that’s enough for us.”
This time, silence didn’t fall.
Choi Minwoo’s words had made everything clear.
They trusted Jin Taekyung.
The simple certainty in those words swept away even the faint doubts and denials everyone had kept hidden in their hearts.
Even when everything around you is dark, you can still see the torch moving ahead.
And to them—no, to all humanity—Jin Taekyung was the one torch burning brighter than any other.
“Right. I had it wrong for a moment.”
Magic Johnson muttered to himself, then let out a small laugh.
“Still, I never thought my greatest wish would be answered like this.”
“Your wish?”
“I couldn’t make sense of anything about you, Jin. I wanted to talk you into letting me run all kinds of experiments on you. Maybe even a little dissection, if you agreed...”
Jin Taekyung asked in all sincerity, “Are you insane?”
“Don’t worry. I’m not planning to do that anymore. Good grief, you said it was a System? My poor imagination never got that far.”
“I don’t think anyone would’ve imagined that.”
Song Song, sitting alone among the mountain-sized men, gestured with her eyes toward the seat beside her.
“Look at Uncle Kkeokjeong. He’s practically out of his mind.”
Every eye turned to Im Kkeokjeong. Still looking dazed, he jumped as though he’d just woken up.
“Huh? Wh-what? Why me? I’m fine.”
“You don’t look fine.”
“No, I was just... listening.”
Im Kkeokjeong scratched the back of his head as he struggled to get the words out.
“Honestly, I’m not sure I should even be hearing something this incredible.”
“Yeah, I feel the same. Team Leader Choi here—no, our Guild Master—has every right to hear it. But us? Well...”
Jin Taekyung gave a quiet laugh at their reactions.
“What’s this about having a right? I called you because you belong here.”
And they did.
They might not have known one another for a large part of their lives, but they were friends and comrades who’d been together through some of the hardest, most turbulent times.
There were others he wanted to call but couldn’t.
People like Butler Kim, who had passed away, or Faye Chen.
Or his family, who couldn’t accept a situation like this, and Seong Jinho, his closest friend since his days at the goshiwon.
“Oh, that’s kind of touching. Didn’t know you could say things like that.”
“I’m pretty good at it, if I do say so myself.”
“Then what were you thinking when we first met? Remember that night we were drinking, and you started going on about Taurus and—”
“...I was wrong.”
Starting with that shameful memory, words came pouring in from every direction.
Some were about little things they could barely remember. Others were as vivid as if they’d happened yesterday.
For a while, they laughed and talked together.
None of them said it aloud, but they all felt it.
This might be the last time they faced one another with smiles like these.
Maybe that was why Jin Taekyung couldn’t bring himself to speak when the time came to say goodbye.
Tick. Tick.
At some point, the sound of a second hand reached him through his keen senses. Jin Taekyung closed his eyes.
The broken pocket watch.
It was moving—the thing that likely linked the modern world and Murim through the absolute power of time.
*I have to leave. Before it’s too late.*
He knew it in his head and in his heart.
Even so, he felt more conflicted than ever.
Before him were faces he was always glad to see. The faces of precious people he hadn’t been able to see hovered before his eyes like mist.
*If only this moment could last forever.*
But it couldn’t.
Time would keep moving. So would the enemy waiting for him in another world.
Unless someone stopped him, he always would.
*That’s why I have to go.*
It was the one thing he had to do.
The one thing only he could do.
Jin Taekyung reminded himself of that unchanging truth and opened his eyes. Everyone was looking at him.
As though they’d instinctively sensed that it was time to part.
“Go on, human. Don’t make a whole thing out of it.”
The Undead King made it sound as though Jin were just popping over to the neighbor’s house. Jin Taekyung couldn’t help laughing.
He looked at the smiling faces before him. Then, thinking of those who must be desperately searching for him somewhere, he said goodbye.
“I’ll come back. I promise.”
Muttering the words like a vow to himself, Jin Taekyung logged in.
Deep in the darkness, a being suddenly awoke and drew a deep breath.
Like a child opening its eyes for the first time in a new world.
Or a pitiful evil spirit struggling to feel that it was still alive.
But this time was different.
The air around him. The qi. All of it.

His breath, always ragged and labored, like that of someone on the verge of death, was calm. And a strength and vitality he hadn’t felt in decades welled up in his body, which had been as good as dead.
Slowly, but without stopping.
The loyal servant who had been waiting alone for her master in the darkness and silence could sense the change, too.
“Congratulations, great Lord of Heaven.”
The Grand Sorceress’s voice trembled. She had always been so composed.
Moments earlier, she had recognized the source of a sudden feeling of déjà vu. She’d come here without hesitation to wait for her master.
“This lowly servant dared to wait for her master without permission. Please punish me.”
The next moment, an answer rang out—one she’d thought she would never hear.
It came not as a sound, but from deep within the Grand Sorceress’s mind.
—You are forgiven.
It could scarcely be called a voice. It was cold as ice, yet the Grand Sorceress trembled with joy.
She’d been right.
The strange sensation she’d felt a moment ago was real. After only a few days, her master had awoken again, having regained even greater power.
And all of this could mean only one thing.
“Has it finally been completed?”
—Far from it.
The Grand Sorceress let out a regretful groan before she could stop herself. Then another reverberation filled her mind, and she caught her breath.
—But it will be completed.
“Then...”
—Nothing can stop what has already begun. No one.
At that pronouncement, like an oracle, the Grand Sorceress—prostrated with all five limbs on the ground, unable to dare face her master—bowed even lower.
Cold seeped up from the damp stone floor, but she didn’t care. The fierce emotion rising deep within her warmed her body like a ball of fire.
“Please give your command. What should this lowly servant do?”
Her joy was plain in the question. Her master answered in a voice that none could hear.
Not the eternal snows of the Tianshan Mountains. Not the sky touching their peaks, nor the moon and stars beyond.
Nor the countless armies crossing the vast continent, finally nearing the Land of Ruin beyond the desert, could hear the voice.

“I understand.
I thought the same thing for a long time.”
Jin Taekyung meant every word.
He hadn’t experienced the Great Cataclysm firsthand, but he’d been born on its final day.
Growing up, he’d been taught about it until he was sick of hearing it: what had happened during the Great Cataclysm, and how humanity had survived.
And how the ruler of the Demon Realm who had caused the Great Cataclysm met his end at the hands of a great hero born of humanity, without leaving so much as a trace.
But...
“He’s alive.
I’m certain of it.
In another world, under the name Lord of Heaven.”
Just as Cheon Taemin had existed as the Martial God, the king of demons had gained a new name in another world.
The beginning and the end of all this.
Jin Taekyung was certain.
To reach the end of the path he’d walked—and the path still ahead of him—he had to reach that bastard.
But no one else could see the shape of the enormous puzzle he’d pieced together while traveling between two worlds.
They could only trust the young man standing before them.
And someone did.
“I see.
Understood.”
Choi Minwoo’s voice was calm.
That made it sound all the more unnatural.
As Cheon Taemin’s only direct blood relative, Choi Minwoo had more reason than anyone there to be shaken by what he’d heard.
His gaze passed briefly over the others, then settled on Jin Taekyung.
It didn’t waver in the slightest.
“If that’s what you believe, Mr.
Jin, that’s enough for us.”
This time, silence didn’t fall.
Choi Minwoo’s words had made everything clear.
They trusted Jin Taekyung.
The simple certainty in those words swept away even the faint doubts and denials everyone had kept hidden in their hearts.
Even when everything around you is dark, you can still see the torch moving ahead.
And to them—no, to all humanity—Jin Taekyung was the one torch burning brighter than any other.
“Right.
I had it wrong for a moment.”
Magic Johnson muttered to himself, then let out a small laugh.
“Still, I never thought my greatest wish would be answered like this.”
“Your wish?”
“I couldn’t make sense of anything about you, Jin.
I wanted to talk you into letting me run all kinds of experiments on you.
Maybe even a little dissection, if you agreed...”
Jin Taekyung asked in all sincerity, “Are you insane?”
“Don’t worry.
I’m not planning to do that anymore.
Good grief, you said it was a System?
My poor imagination never got that far.”
“I don’t think anyone would’ve imagined that.”
Song Song, sitting alone among the mountain-sized men, gestured with her eyes toward the seat beside her.
“Look at Uncle Kkeokjeong.
He’s practically out of his mind.”
Every eye turned to Im Kkeokjeong.
Still looking dazed, he jumped as though he’d just woken up.
“Huh?
Wh-what?
Why me?
I’m fine.”
“You don’t look fine.”
“No, I was just... listening.”
Im Kkeokjeong scratched the back of his head as he struggled to get the words out.
“Honestly, I’m not sure I should even be hearing something this incredible.”
“Yeah, I feel the same.
Team Leader Choi here—no, our Guild Master—has every right to hear it.
But us?
Well...”
Jin Taekyung gave a quiet laugh at their reactions.
“What’s this about having a right?
I called you because you belong here.”
And they did.
They might not have known one another for a large part of their lives, but they were friends and comrades who’d been together through some of the hardest, most turbulent times.
There were others he wanted to call but couldn’t.
People like Butler Kim, who had passed away, or Faye Chen.
Or his family, who couldn’t accept a situation like this, and Seong Jinho, his closest friend since his days at the goshiwon.
“Oh, that’s kind of touching.
Didn’t know you could say things like that.”
“I’m pretty good at it, if I do say so myself.”
“Then what were you thinking when we first met?
Remember that night we were drinking, and you started going on about Taurus and—”
“...I was wrong.”
Starting with that shameful memory, words came pouring in from every direction.
Some were about little things they could barely remember.
Others were as vivid as if they’d happened yesterday.
For a while, they laughed and talked together.
None of them said it aloud, but they all felt it.
This might be the last time they faced one another with smiles like these.
Maybe that was why Jin Taekyung couldn’t bring himself to speak when the time came to say goodbye.
Tick.
Tick.
At some point, the sound of a second hand reached him through his keen senses.
Jin Taekyung closed his eyes.
The broken pocket watch.
It was moving—the thing that likely linked the modern world and Murim through the absolute power of time.
*I have to leave.
Before it’s too late.*
He knew it in his head and in his heart.
Even so, he felt more conflicted than ever.
Before him were faces he was always glad to see.
The faces of precious people he hadn’t been able to see hovered before his eyes like mist.
*If only this moment could last forever.*
But it couldn’t.
Time would keep moving.
So would the enemy waiting for him in another world.
Unless someone stopped him, he always would.
*That’s why I have to go.*
It was the one thing he had to do.
The one thing only he could do.
Jin Taekyung reminded himself of that unchanging truth and opened his eyes.
Everyone was looking at him.
As though they’d instinctively sensed that it was time to part.
“Go on, human.
Don’t make a whole thing out of it.”
The Undead King made it sound as though Jin were just popping over to the neighbor’s house.
Jin Taekyung couldn’t help laughing.
He looked at the smiling faces before him.
Then, thinking of those who must be desperately searching for him somewhere, he said goodbye.
“I’ll come back.
I promise.”
Muttering the words like a vow to himself, Jin Taekyung logged in.
Deep in the darkness, a being suddenly awoke and drew a deep breath.
Like a child opening its eyes for the first time in a new world.
Or a pitiful evil spirit struggling to feel that it was still alive.
But this time was different.
The air around him.
The qi.
All of it.
His breath, always ragged and labored, like that of someone on the verge of death, was calm.
And a strength and vitality he hadn’t felt in decades welled up in his body, which had been as good as dead.
Slowly, but without stopping.
The loyal servant who had been waiting alone for her master in the darkness and silence could sense the change, too.
“Congratulations, great Lord of Heaven.”
The Grand Sorceress’s voice trembled.
She had always been so composed.
Moments earlier, she had recognized the source of a sudden feeling of déjà vu.
She’d come here without hesitation to wait for her master.
“This lowly servant dared to wait for her master without permission.
Please punish me.”
The next moment, an answer rang out—one she’d thought she would never hear.
It came not as a sound, but from deep within the Grand Sorceress’s mind.
—You are forgiven.
It could scarcely be called a voice.
It was cold as ice, yet the Grand Sorceress trembled with joy.
She’d been right.
The strange sensation she’d felt a moment ago was real.
After only a few days, her master had awoken again, having regained even greater power.
And all of this could mean only one thing.
“Has it finally been completed?”
—Far from it.
The Grand Sorceress let out a regretful groan before she could stop herself.
Then another reverberation filled her mind, and she caught her breath.
—But it will be completed.
“Then...”
—Nothing can stop what has already begun.
No one.
At that pronouncement, like an oracle, the Grand Sorceress—prostrated with all five limbs on the ground, unable to dare face her master—bowed even lower.
Cold seeped up from the damp stone floor, but she didn’t care.
The fierce emotion rising deep within her warmed her body like a ball of fire.
“Please give your command.
What should this lowly servant do?”
Her joy was plain in the question.
Her master answered in a voice that none could hear.
Not the eternal snows of the Tianshan Mountains.
Not the sky touching their peaks, nor the moon and stars beyond.
Nor the countless armies crossing the vast continent, finally nearing the Land of Ruin beyond the desert, could hear the voice.

chapters.title: Chapter 1176
paragraphs: Login—or Logout.
Like the games I played as a kid, crossing an invisible boundary between two worlds had become familiar to me.
The moment everything around me vanished and my vision went dark, I found myself alone.
In darkness so deep I couldn’t see an inch ahead.
Of course, it never lasted long.
An unknown force would soon take hold of my consciousness and lead it somewhere. At the end of that journey, the light of a new world would be waiting.
But why?
*Something’s different.*
I sensed it instinctively. What startled me was that even after the thought crossed my mind, the darkness remained.
*Why?*
The process, the sensations—both had become as familiar as breathing. Now they felt strange.
By now, my consciousness should have crossed from the modern world into Murim. Then I would regain my usual senses and awareness in the other body I’d been apart from. That was the routine.
But this time, everything was different.
The darkness and silence went on for what felt like an eternity.
Then, at the end of that suffocating wait, came the pull.
*Whoooosh.*
As if caught in a massive tornado, my consciousness was sucked toward depths I couldn’t begin to fathom.
I clung with all my strength to the thread of my consciousness as a pull more powerful than anything I’d ever felt threatened to shake it loose.
*Damn it. What the hell is this?*
If my previous trips had been rides in a limousine, this one was a locomotive.
A broken-down runaway locomotive hurtling down rusted, misaligned tracks, with no engineer to control its speed.
*Stop!*
The cry rang out in my mind before I could help it.
But a school bully rotten to the core wouldn’t stop tormenting someone at a single shout. Neither did the powerful wave carrying my consciousness toward who knew where.
And at the end of that insane ride—
*Whooosh!*
Darkness split apart as though torn open. A shaft of light brighter than any I’d seen before burst through and swallowed my vision.
With it came a voice, carried to me through senses that had snapped sharply into focus.
“You’ve come back.”
He hadn’t asked if I was awake.
He’d asked if I’d come back.
Leaving the frantic ordeal behind me, I slowly opened my eyes and looked at the owner of the voice.
Bells were ringing one after another, beginning with a System message announcing that Login had succeeded. But his voice fell on my ears like spring rain.
“Yes, Master.”
*Master.*
At the ease with which the title came from my lips, the Fire King, Jeok Cheongang, widened his eyes.
Then they curved gently, like a full moon.
“Yes. Good to have you back.”
At long last, I was in Murim.
The joy of our reunion was brief.
More precisely, there was no need to draw it out.
People who knew each other better than anyone else didn’t need many words. Jeok Cheongang and I had been like that for a long time.
And for that very reason, he must have noticed right away that something was wrong with me.
“So, what kind of dogshit situation has happened this time?”
“Are you psychic? How’d you know?”
“Look at yourself. How could I not?”
“What about me? I—oh.”
Only then did I realize I was drenched in cold sweat.
It had soaked through my clothes and even the bedding beneath me. So much for having reached the realm of Unaffected by Cold and Heat a long time ago.
“When did this start?”
“A little while ago. You were groaning so much I thought you might shit yourself.”
Where had that warm feeling from a moment ago gone? Was it just me, or did the air smell like a public restroom now?
I grimaced and answered, “Hard to say. More than one thing comes to mind. Anyway, where’s everyone else?”
That was what I’d wanted to ask first.
No matter how I looked around, Jeok Cheongang was the only face I could see. And aside from the snorting of the horses pulling us along, I couldn’t sense anyone nearby.
His answer made my already-prickling nerves go cold.
“Gone.”
My heart dropped with a thud. That was exactly how it felt.
“Gone?” I asked, my voice trembling.
“I said they’re gone.”
“So they were here, but—”
“Ah, they’re gone! Right now!”
Jeok Cheongang snapped, then continued.
“To be precise, they all left about one shichen ago. They needed to scout the area and find a place to camp tonight. They’ll probably be back soon.”
What the hell?
I stared at him in silence. My heart had long since returned to its proper place.
“You should’ve said that first.”
“Look at this disrespectful brat. You’re the one who didn’t listen to the end. How’s that my fault?”
As Jeok Cheongang glared at me, I turned my head slightly to the side.
Outside the large, beautiful eight-horse carriage the emperor of the Great Nation—no, the Great Ming Empire—had bestowed on me alone, darkness covered the world.
“By the way, where are we...?”
“Xinjiang.”
Xinjiang.
The vastest land under heaven, and a Land of Ruin no one had dared invade for ages.
While I’d been away from Murim, the journey that began in Qinghai had finally brought us here.
Even now, grains of sand trickled through the gaps in the carriage, proof that we were deep in the heart of Xinjiang.
“The Taklamakan Desert.”
Jeok Cheongang muttered the name, then spat out the sand that had gotten into his mouth.
“Damn desert. When I think of all the hell I’ve been through for nearly a month, I really...”
I didn’t hear the rest.
Not because he’d trailed off, or because of the fierce sandstorm beating against the carriage window.
*A month. A whole month has already passed?*
I’d spent less than a week in the modern world.
Yet a month had passed in Murim during those few days.
*The axis of time has gone out of alignment. Beyond the point of no return.*
I’d already suspected as much.
When I returned to the modern world after fighting the Blood Lord in Qinghai, I’d realized the time ratio was badly off.
But foreboding was one thing when it stayed in my head. Seeing it become reality was another.
Tick. Tick.
The cold ticking of the [Broken Pocket Watch] I’d tucked deep in my Inventory just before logging in seemed to ring in my ears like a phantom sound.
*But... maybe it’s a good thing this much time has passed. It means we’re that much closer to our destination.*
A month was no short stretch of time.
Especially given the situation the world faced now.
But unlike the modern world, which had suffered terrible damage in just ten days since Morgoth’s arrival, there hadn’t been any significant damage here yet.
Or at least, that was how it felt at the moment.
Whether I’d still think so after asking my next question was another matter.
“While I was asleep, did anything...?”
“You mean, did anything happen? No. Nothing out of the ordinary.”
Jeok Cheongang answered without hesitation, as if he’d known what I was going to ask. His voice dropped as he added, “It’s so peaceful it feels strange.”
“What do you mean?”
“Just what I said. The sky is murky and impossible to predict. One moment it’s snow or rain, the next it’s heat that could melt you, or even hail. But aside from that, there’s nothing.”
That wasn’t particularly surprising.
The sudden climate changes were happening in both the modern world and Murim, and they were nothing new by now.
Besides, this was Xinjiang, where the Lord of Heaven had holed up. If anything, the changes here would be worse, not better.
What caught my attention was the last thing Jeok Cheongang had said.
“Nothing at all?”
“That’s right. None of us thought much of it on the first day. But it didn’t take long for everyone, this old man included, to notice.”
And when Jeok Cheongang went on to explain, I realized there wasn’t the slightest exaggeration or lie in what he’d said.
“At first, nobody paid it any mind. We were busy taking turns scouting the area every half shichen and standing watch through the night.”
That was only natural.
This was Xinjiang.
The thousand-year Sacred Land of the Hundred Thousand Demonic Disciples, who’d once swept across the land, and the base of Dark Heaven.
Dark Heaven had unleashed bloodshed across the Central Plains. It wouldn’t have been surprising if they’d turned Xinjiang, practically their own front yard, into a sea of blood.

“But strangely, it was quiet. None of those crazy fanatics who’d swarmed us like a pack of dogs in Qinghai. None of those monsters that defied all reason. Not even a band of common mounted bandits. At first, I thought maybe the bastards were scared.”
It wasn’t arrogance or carelessness that had led him to think so.

Just before we set out from Qinghai, the emperor and the leaders of the alliance army—the foremost figures of Murim—had divided a force of well over a hundred thousand into three groups. We were one of them.
Our group numbered fewer than twenty. But look at who was in it.
Two Stars and the strongest of the Ten Kings.
The Bow Saint, the Slaughter Saint, and the Fire King, who stood shoulder to shoulder with them.
Even with me unconscious, those three alone were more than enough to be called an army.
“But the very next day, I realized I’d been wrong from the start.”
Jeok Cheongang muttered in a low voice, then suddenly jerked his chin toward the window.
“Do you see?”
“What are you—”
I frowned at the gesture, then stopped mid-sentence.
In that instant, I understood.
Beyond the window, the vast desert stretched into the darkness, filled with nothing but sand.
At the same time, not a sound could be heard.
“Could it be...?”
“That’s right.”
Jeok Cheongang continued, his voice heavy and subdued.
“There isn’t a single living thing in this land.”

chapters.title: Chapter 1177
paragraphs: A land of death.
Just as the name said, a place utterly devoid of life.
The truth I’d failed to notice came over me with the chill of a blade pressed to the back of my neck.
*No living things at all? How is that possible?*
I swallowed the question almost as soon as it sprang to mind.
It was a foolish question.
If the Lord of Heaven—no, the Demon King Asmodeus—stood at the beginning and end of all this, then it was even less surprising.
He’d dragged an apocalypse that had existed only in people’s imaginations into reality. From the moment I learned what he was, *common sense* had lost all meaning.
Another question quickly took the first one’s place. One that was more practical, and closer to the heart of the matter.
I stared out the window. Not a bird called. Not an insect chirped.
“What’s the purpose?”
It was far too late to ask *how*.
What mattered to me now—to us—was why.
And it seemed the person hiding in the sandstorm that had blown in from far away, whose presence had settled on the carriage roof a moment earlier, knew that too.
“One of two things.”
The Slaughter Saint’s voice was boyishly young, yet carried a bleakness that spoke of all the years he’d lived.
“The first is a final battle. Gathering everything in Xinjiang for one last fight.”
“Then the second is...”

“I don’t know exactly what happened, but the whole of Xinjiang has lost the breath of life. People and animals have legs; they could have gone elsewhere. But even the plants across the region have withered. Dark Heaven’s probably behind it.”
Jeok Cheongang cut in gruffly.
“Eavesdropping like a rat, only to tell us something that goes without saying.”
“Watch your mouth. That rat might cut your throat tonight.”
“I wouldn’t mind. We’re running low on food. Roast rat, nice and crisp, would make a fine breakfast tomorrow.”
“That mouth of yours never gets any better. What the hell have you done with all the years you’ve lived?”
With that curt reply, a shadow fell across the window.

Like a ghost with no substance, the Slaughter Saint passed through the window as if it weren’t there and entered the carriage. He stared at me as though he could see straight through whatever I was hiding.
“Anyway, you slept a long time.”
I smacked my lips.
I’d been traveling with the Slaughter Saint for quite a while, but this was the first time I’d been gone for a whole month. And by any ordinary measure, no one could sleep for an entire month.
But what could I do? The day would come when I told him the truth myself. For now, I’d have to bluff with a straight face.
“Yeah, I sleep a lot.”
“Even so, it’s impossible to stay asleep for a month.”
“I’ve got an unusual constitution.”
“I’ve wandered the land for fifty years and seen all kinds of patients. No such constitution exists.”
“Congratulations. After fifty years, you’ve discovered a new one.”
A suffocating silence filled the carriage. The Slaughter Saint and even Jeok Cheongang stared at me as if I were a madman.
Fair enough. You didn’t need medical training to know that was nonsense.
“I’m kidding. I did wake up a few times in between. You know, to take care of basic bodily functions and all that.”
“I didn’t know that.”
“Of course not. Only Master knew. Right?”
Jeok Cheongang blinked at my sudden plea for help, then scratched the back of his head.
“Uh. Well, that is...”
His reaction was a little odd, but the most important thing when lying was to sound natural. I kept talking before the Slaughter Saint could notice.
“I woke up once a few days ago, too. After sleeping so long, I had to pee, and I was hungry.”
“When exactly was that?”
“Um... I wasn’t fully awake, so I don’t really know.”
“I see.”
The Slaughter Saint nodded as if he understood, then muttered to himself.
“Strange. You woke up several times, and nobody noticed.”
“Yeah. Strange, isn’t it?”
“Something even stranger happened. Would you like to hear it?”
Was it just my imagination, or had the air gone a little stale?
Uneasy for some reason, I shook my head.
“...No. Not really.”
“Surely you’re curious.”
“I’m fine. Sometimes it’s better not to know.”
“A good saying. But another one fits this situation better.”
The Slaughter Saint’s voice was gentler than usual, which made it all the more ominous.
“That mouth of yours is asking for a beating.”
“What do you think?”
What was I supposed to think?
I forced a smile.
“Now I’m very curious. I’d love to hear what happened.”
“Taken on its own, it’s nothing remarkable. From where I stood, it was mostly a nuisance.”
“What do you mean...?”

“What a close Master and Disciple you are. From the first day of our journey, a certain ill-tempered old man raised hell unless I checked on you morning and evening. Not a single day went by in peace.”
The Slaughter Saint’s eyes sank as he glared at Jeok Cheongang, as though just remembering it exhausted him.
“Lately, his fits reached new heights. You’d been asleep for nearly a month, so he decided something must be wrong. He shouted at me, demanding to know why I couldn’t find the problem.”
“That was only two days ago. Anything to say?”
You’ve got to be kidding me.
Of course I had nothing.
I knew something had felt off. Now I understood Jeok Cheongang’s strange reaction earlier.
Under the Slaughter Saint’s stare—and mine—Jeok Cheongang looked out the window and muttered, “Well, I didn’t shout *that* much...”
“You even called me a quack.”
“I didn’t put it quite that directly...”
“True. You were a little more roundabout. You asked if I’d learned medicine at a gambling den.”
“I did say that, but it wasn’t so harsh...”
“And what possessed you to accuse me of trying to live up to my title as the Slaughter Saint by killing your Disciple?”
“Hmm. I suppose I went too far there. My pride won’t let me apologize, so I’ll offer my regrets instead.”
The answer was steeped in the essence of the Fire Gate Clan—a clan that had been making Murim’s people furious on a regular basis for more than three hundred years. A sound almost escaped me.
Then I saw the Slaughter Saint’s expression and held it in with everything I had.
“You fucking—!”
I was very relieved Cheongpung wasn’t here.

If he’d seen this, he would’ve spouted some nonsense like, *Wow! I’ve never seen the greatest assassin of all time swear before!* Then I would’ve had to watch the greatest assassin of all time lose his temper and go on a rampage.

Fortunately, the man with another identity as the Divine Physician knew how to keep to a minimum standard of decency—unlike my dear Master—and, as a former assassin, had a near-supernatural skill for recovering his composure.
“Fine. Yes... It happens. People close to a patient sometimes can’t think clearly. It happens. I understand.”
After muttering as if trying to hypnotize himself, the Slaughter Saint took a steadying breath and turned to me.
Then he asked something I could never have anticipated.
“So, did you take care of things over there?”
“What?”
“Your hometown. The realm of immortals, wasn’t it?”
For a moment, the world seemed to stop.
If not for the carriage’s constant rattling, the sand slipping through the window, and Jeok Cheongang’s conspicuously deliberate clearing of his throat, I might have believed it had.
“Ahem. Well, that’s how it happened.”
*That happened. That happened. That happened...*
His words seemed to echo, though we weren’t in some deep mountain valley. I closed my eyes for a moment, then opened them and looked at Jeok Cheongang.
He was trying very hard to look stern.
I said nothing. I just kept looking at him.
“W-why are you looking at me like that?”
“Well, I couldn’t help it. You’d been out cold for a whole month. I was worried, and the Slaughter Saint kept getting suspicious...”
“I only explained a little! Just a little! He’s a physician. When he asks about a patient, he ought to know *something* about the patient’s condition!”
I let out a long sigh at his halting excuses.
“I understand.”
“You’d always woken up after a few days at most. This time, I even wondered if you’d been poisoned with some sleeping drug from the demonic, heterodox arts... What did you say?”
“I said I understand. You had your reasons.”
Well, what was done was done.
Maybe it was just me, but I’d grown pretty close to the Slaughter Saint. He was one of my most dependable allies, too. He deserved to know my secret.
To be honest, part of me was relieved it was out.

Besides, the decision had been made by my Master. Jeok Cheongang must have had his reasons. If he’d slept for a whole month like a bear hibernating through winter, even I would have started to suspect something.
Anyway...
“How much did you tell him about me?”
“Hmm. Well...”
Why did I suddenly feel a chill?
I’d only asked in case I needed to fill in the details, but Jeok Cheongang hesitated and glanced at me before answering.
“I told them more or less what I knew. Their reactions varied at first, but they all believed me.”
“Oh, that’s fine. I was planning to tell him soon anyway... Wait. Their reactions varied?”
That was strange.
There was only one of him. How could there be several reactions?
A shout from somewhere in the distance answered my question.
“Waaah! Benefactor! You’re back! Did you have a good trip?”
Ah.

chapters.title: Chapter 1178
paragraphs: There’s no such thing as a perfect secret.
Birds hear what’s said by day, rats hear what’s said by night, and sooner or later, it all comes out of someone’s mouth.
“I swear to Heaven, this old man told exactly one person.”
The culprit who’d first let my secret slip made his declaration like a newborn letting out its first cry. At that, the “one person” in question licked his lips.
“Well, I was only going to check a few facts. How was I supposed to believe a word that crazy old man said?”
“And then?” I asked quietly.
“I had no choice but to corner the person who seemed to know you best and ask him.”
The Slaughter Saint’s gaze shifted to Hyuk Mujin. Huddled in a corner of the carriage, Mujin had been watching everyone’s reactions. Now he stammered out an answer.
“To be precise, you kidnapped me in the dead of night while I was sound asleep and buried me in the desert. With only my head sticking out.”
“That’s right. But he turned out to be surprisingly tight-lipped. He insisted he’d rather die than tell me anything that might put you in danger.”
Perhaps buoyed by the Slaughter Saint’s testimony, Hyuk Mujin straightened his hunched shoulders.
“You heard him, right? That’s how loyal I am.”
“So, I had no choice but to tell him a rough version of what I’d heard. Then the very next day, some random weirdo came asking about you.”
Right on cue, that “random fool” poked his head in.
“Benefactor! Benefactor! You really came from the realm of immortals? It’s true? Wow! I’ve never met anyone from the realm of immortals before!”
“Yeah. Just like that.”
The Slaughter Saint gave Cheongpung a tired glare, then added, “Anyway, I only told one person, too.”
Hyuk Mujin drew his shoulders in again and muttered, “So did I.”
Yeah. Of course he had.
But if I were Hyuk Mujin, I wouldn’t have shared a “stupendous secret I couldn’t possibly keep to myself” with Cheongpung.
Why? Simple.
Because he was Cheongpung.
“Benefactor, me too! I only told Young Lady Ju!”
Maybe an innocence-proving contest had started without my noticing. Cheongpung shouted with tremendous enthusiasm, and Jeok Cheongang nodded.
“He’s not wrong. The problem was that he said it at just about that volume, at a meal where most of us were gathered.”
This was giving me a headache.
I shook my head and happened to meet someone’s eyes.
Unlike the others, she’d been silent this whole time, without so much as a reaction. Ju Hwaran.
“Ah, Young Lady Ju.”
I greeted her with an awkward smile, but she didn’t answer.
She only stared at me, her gaze pricking my face like a thin needle.
No, she wasn’t the only one looking at me.
A hush had fallen over the carriage. Everyone was watching.
Well. I didn’t know.
I felt like I should say something, but what? And how?
*Should I act like nothing happened? Or apologize for not telling them sooner...?*
My thoughts were tangling like a ball of yarn when her tightly closed red lips parted.
“You’re not, are you?”
“Huh? What do you mean, all of a sudden?”
“You’re not actually an immortal or something instead of a human, are you?”
“An immortal?”
I blinked at her. Then I understood and let out a small, disbelieving laugh.
“Come on. Do I look that impressive to you, Young Lady Ju?”
“Don’t laugh.”
“...Sorry. I couldn’t help it. But I’m really not.”
“Are you sure?”
“Of course. What else would I be if not human? A few misunderstandings piled up, and somehow my home came to be called the realm of immortals. But people live there just like they do here.”
“Really?”
“Yes.”
Calling the two worlds the same would be a huge stretch.
Even setting aside the difference in technology, at least around here you wouldn’t run into a monster on your way to the inn at the intersection near your house.
But I didn’t bother explaining that, and Ju Hwaran didn’t seem inclined to press the point.
Instead, she asked another question I hadn’t expected.
“Then how old are you really?”
“...Where did that come from?”
“I’m just curious. You said only your soul goes back and forth, and your world is different from this one.”
I answered, still a little bewildered.
“Uh, well. Around twenty-eight?”
“Around?”
“No, that’s right. Going back and forth a few times has messed up my sense of time, so I got confused for a second...”
I’d started rambling out excuses without meaning to when Ju Hwaran cut me off in a voice as sharp as a blade.
“So you haven’t even turned thirty yet.”
“That’s right.”
“And you’re not an immortal or a celestial who’s lived for five hundred years since ascending to immortality.”
“...I told you, I’m human.”
Ascended to immortality? Please.
I’d been called an idiot plenty of times. By Hayeon.
And if I really were a five-hundred-year-old immortal, the one pulling this eight-horse carriage right now would be the Lord of Heaven, not a horse.
*Wouldn’t that be nice?*
I was lost in that sweet, sad thought when Ju Hwaran delivered her verdict like a judge who’d finished hearing the case.
“That settles it, then.”
“Huh?”
“It’s fine. You’re human, and you’re around twenty-eight.”
It was a strange verdict.
No account of the case. No sentence.
But that was enough.
I didn’t know what it was, but it was settled.
*No, honestly, I think I do know.*
For some reason, my chest felt tight. Somewhere close to my heart.
At the same time, another part of it grew heavy.
Was it okay to feel this way right now? Did I have any right to?
Maybe that was why I found it hard to meet her eyes as she kept looking steadily at me, with everyone else watching us and making the air between us stranger still.
And why, the next moment, I changed the subject for no good reason.
“Anyway, when will the others be back?”
“H-hm?”
“The people who aren’t here.”
Jeok Cheongang, who’d been looking back and forth between Ju Hwaran and me, cleared his throat.
“Ahem. Why do you ask all of a sudden?”
“I want to see them. And now that it’s come to this, there’s something I’d like to tell everyone myself.”
“Well, they’re searching different areas, so they’ll all be back before long. But there’s no need to gather them for that. Some of them still don’t know anything about you.”
“What? But earlier, that human Cheongpung clearly—”
“Yes, that careless mouth of his said it loud enough for everyone to hear. At a meal where *most* of us were gathered.”
“Oh.”
I let out a short exclamation.
At the same time, it wasn’t hard to think of the person most likely not to have heard my secret yet.
“Great Sir.”
The Supreme Peak master we’d first met in Gansu, who’d accompanied us all the way here.
A mysterious eccentric as baffling as his wild, unkempt hair. Even he didn’t know who he was.
“What Great Sir? The fellow loses his mind several times a day.”
Jeok Cheongang snorted, then continued.

“If he’d happened to be there, we couldn’t have helped it. But it still didn’t sit right with this old man to go out of my way to tell him, so I told everyone to keep quiet. He’s been quite useful, but a secret is a secret, and we don’t even know who he is.”
“Hmm.”
“I can guess what you’re thinking. I’m not going to force my judgment on you. Do as you like about that fellow you call Great Sir. But...”
Jeok Cheongang trailed off and scratched his bushy beard.
“There’s someone else I’m more concerned about than him.”
“Someone else?”
“The ones here have more or less understood and accepted it by now. But things don’t always work out so neatly. Old folks especially have trouble understanding anything new.”
Just as I’d thought of Great Sir, I remembered another person who wasn’t here.
*Bow Saint.*
I muttered the words to myself and looked out the window.
Perhaps because clouds were passing across the pitch-black sky, the stars looked especially dim tonight.
Desert nights were merciless.
By day, the heat seemed ready to burn the whole world. Once the sun set and darkness fell, an icy chill blanketed the land.
Yet even in the cold that seeped to the bone, the slender shadow cast alone atop a sand dune did not waver.
That was only natural. The master who cast it had long since surpassed the realm of Unaffected by Cold and Heat.
But that wasn’t the only reason.
“The realm of immortals... The realm of immortals.”
Bow Saint gazed into the dark desert, her eyes clouded with thought.
The boundless sea of sand before her seemed to mirror her heart.
No end in sight, no matter how far she walked. Nothing within it but hardship and rough grains of sand.
“So that was the secret you were hiding.”
She murmured the words softly.
The desert at night was an excellent listener.
It asked no questions. It only let the wind pass through in silence, from wherever that wind had come.
But it was no good for conversation.
No, even if the desert could speak, that wouldn’t change.
The person the Bow Saint wanted to speak to was someone else.
“...Martial God.”
Her fingers, hard as steel and callused despite her translucent skin, searched inside her robe.
Through the fabric, they found the old letter the Martial God had left for her alone, containing a secret she therefore could tell no one.
“Is this what you want?”
The Bow Saint could not understand.
She had trusted and followed the letter’s instructions only because the Martial God had left it. From the beginning until now, she had never been able to make sense of what it said.
And after hearing Jin Taekyung’s secret just a few days ago, she found it even harder to understand.
“Is this truly... right?”
At that moment—
*Rustle.*
A faint sound behind her reached the Bow Saint’s ears.

“You’re not actually an immortal or something instead of a human, are you?”
“An immortal?”
I blinked at her.
Then I understood and let out a small, disbelieving laugh.
“Come on.
Do I look that impressive to you, Young Lady Ju?”
“Don’t laugh.”
“...Sorry.
I couldn’t help it.
But I’m really not.”
“Are you sure?”
“Of course.
What else would I be if not human?
A few misunderstandings piled up, and somehow my home came to be called the realm of immortals.
But people live there just like they do here.”
“Really?”
“Yes.”
Calling the two worlds the same would be a huge stretch.
Even setting aside the difference in technology, at least around here you wouldn’t run into a monster on your way to the inn at the intersection near your house.
But I didn’t bother explaining that, and Ju Hwaran didn’t seem inclined to press the point.
Instead, she asked another question I hadn’t expected.
“Then how old are you really?”
“...Where did that come from?”
“I’m just curious.
You said only your soul goes back and forth, and your world is different from this one.”
I answered, still a little bewildered.
“Uh, well.
Around twenty-eight?”
“Around?”
“No, that’s right.
Going back and forth a few times has messed up my sense of time, so I got confused for a second...”
I’d started rambling out excuses without meaning to when Ju Hwaran cut me off in a voice as sharp as a blade.
“So you haven’t even turned thirty yet.”
“That’s right.”
“And you’re not an immortal or a celestial who’s lived for five hundred years since ascending to immortality.”
“...I told you, I’m human.”
Ascended to immortality?
Please.
I’d been called an idiot plenty of times.
By Hayeon.
And if I really were a five-hundred-year-old immortal, the one pulling this eight-horse carriage right now would be the Lord of Heaven, not a horse.
*Wouldn’t that be nice?*
I was lost in that sweet, sad thought when Ju Hwaran delivered her verdict like a judge who’d finished hearing the case.
“That settles it, then.”
“Huh?”
“It’s fine.
You’re human, and you’re around twenty-eight.”
It was a strange verdict.
No account of the case.
No sentence.
But that was enough.
I didn’t know what it was, but it was settled.
*No, honestly, I think I do know.*
For some reason, my chest felt tight.
Somewhere close to my heart.
At the same time, another part of it grew heavy.
Was it okay to feel this way right now?
Did I have any right to?
Maybe that was why I found it hard to meet her eyes as she kept looking steadily at me, with everyone else watching us and making the air between us stranger still.
And why, the next moment, I changed the subject for no good reason.
“Anyway, when will the others be back?”
“H-hm?”
“The people who aren’t here.”
Jeok Cheongang, who’d been looking back and forth between Ju Hwaran and me, cleared his throat.
“Ahem.
Why do you ask all of a sudden?”
“I want to see them.
And now that it’s come to this, there’s something I’d like to tell everyone myself.”
“Well, they’re searching different areas, so they’ll all be back before long.
But there’s no need to gather them for that.
Some of them still don’t know anything about you.”
“What?
But earlier, that human Cheongpung clearly—”
“Yes, that careless mouth of his said it loud enough for everyone to hear.
At a meal where *most* of us were gathered.”
“Oh.”
I let out a short exclamation.
At the same time, it wasn’t hard to think of the person most likely not to have heard my secret yet.
“Great Sir.”
The Supreme Peak master we’d first met in Gansu, who’d accompanied us all the way here.
A mysterious eccentric as baffling as his wild, unkempt hair.
Even he didn’t know who he was.
“What Great Sir?
The fellow loses his mind several times a day.”
Jeok Cheongang snorted, then continued.
“If he’d happened to be there, we couldn’t have helped it.
But it still didn’t sit right with this old man to go out of my way to tell him, so I told everyone to keep quiet.
He’s been quite useful, but a secret is a secret, and we don’t even know who he is.”
“Hmm.”
“I can guess what you’re thinking.
I’m not going to force my judgment on you.
Do as you like about that fellow you call Great Sir.
But...”
Jeok Cheongang trailed off and scratched his bushy beard.
“There’s someone else I’m more concerned about than him.”
“Someone else?”
“The ones here have more or less understood and accepted it by now.
But things don’t always work out so neatly.
Old folks especially have trouble understanding anything new.”
Just as I’d thought of Great Sir, I remembered another person who wasn’t here.
*Bow Saint.*
I muttered the words to myself and looked out the window.
Perhaps because clouds were passing across the pitch-black sky, the stars looked especially dim tonight.
Desert nights were merciless.
By day, the heat seemed ready to burn the whole world.
Once the sun set and darkness fell, an icy chill blanketed the land.
Yet even in the cold that seeped to the bone, the slender shadow cast alone atop a sand dune did not waver.
That was only natural.
The master who cast it had long since surpassed the realm of Unaffected by Cold and Heat.
But that wasn’t the only reason.
“The realm of immortals...
The realm of immortals.”
Bow Saint gazed into the dark desert, her eyes clouded with thought.
The boundless sea of sand before her seemed to mirror her heart.
No end in sight, no matter how far she walked.
Nothing within it but hardship and rough grains of sand.
“So that was the secret you were hiding.”
She murmured the words softly.
The desert at night was an excellent listener.
It asked no questions.
It only let the wind pass through in silence, from wherever that wind had come.
But it was no good for conversation.
No, even if the desert could speak, that wouldn’t change.
The person the Bow Saint wanted to speak to was someone else.
“...Martial God.”
Her fingers, hard as steel and callused despite her translucent skin, searched inside her robe.
Through the fabric, they found the old letter the Martial God had left for her alone, containing a secret she therefore could tell no one.
“Is this what you want?”
The Bow Saint could not understand.
She had trusted and followed the letter’s instructions only because the Martial God had left it.
From the beginning until now, she had never been able to make sense of what it said.
And after hearing Jin Taekyung’s secret just a few days ago, she found it even harder to understand.
“Is this truly... right?”
At that moment—
*Rustle.*
A faint sound behind her reached the Bow Saint’s ears.

chapters.title: Chapter 1179
paragraphs: Bow Saint reacted at once.
As if she’d expected it, she kicked off the ground and retreated. At the same moment, she thrust a palm wreathed in white Force toward the source of the sound.
*Boom!*
A blinding flash engulfed the sand dune where she had stood alone.
No, there were two of them now.
An uninvited guest had arrived.
*How could I make such a mistake...?*

Normally, she could keep track of everything within twenty-odd zhang without even drawing on her internal energy. Yet she hadn’t noticed an enemy approaching until they were within a dozen zhang. Bow Saint bit her lip.
She’d been too deep in thought. Her heart was more unsettled than ever, and that had surely played a part.
But none of it excused her carelessness. Not here in Xinjiang.
If there were two consolations, the first was that the enemy’s stealth technique was worse than she’d expected. The second was...
“Gwaaah!”
With a strangled scream, the enemy flew into the distance and landed with a wet smack. The back of the figure sprawled there looked rather familiar.
More familiar still was the dreadful stench that had come barging in ahead of him like a thief.
*...That smell.*
As an archer, Bow Saint had eyesight second to none. This time, she hadn’t needed it. Her nose had recognized him first.
The stench was so awful she feared smelling it in her dreams. She wondered how she had failed to notice it until now.
Suppressing a wave of nausea, Bow Saint watched the uninvited guest groan and get to his feet.
“Why are you here?”
There was a trace of suspicion in her voice.
Then, as always, he left her dumbfounded.
“Gah! An enemy! It’s Dark Heaven!”
“Reveal your mask and take off your identity! How dare you ambush this lady! Do you not fear the Lord of Heaven?”
Bow Saint couldn’t hold back any longer. She spoke up, stunned from beginning to end.
“You’ve got it backward.”
“What?”
“You take off a mask, not your identity.”
He wasn’t wearing a mask, either, but she saw no point in explaining that. Even if she went through his mistakes one by one, he’d forget by tomorrow—no, within a shichen.
That man, who referred to himself as “this lady” without a second thought, was Great Sir.
*At least he knows Dark Heaven is the enemy.*
Bow Saint sighed inwardly. Just then, Great Sir finally recognized her, and his eyes widened.
“Wait, why are you here, Young Lady?”
“First, I’m not young enough to be called that. Second, that’s my question for you. I already asked it.”
She added quietly, “And I still haven’t heard an answer.”

The Force around her hand had vanished without a trace, but appearances could be deceiving. Several jiazi’s worth of internal energy continued to circulate within her, faster and more quietly than before, ready to unleash its full power whenever she wished.
One mistake was enough. If she’d made the same mistake twice, she would neither be known as Bow Saint nor have survived the Great Faction War.
“I thought you were supposed to scout somewhere else. Am I mistaken?”
Bow Saint held on to her suspicion.
They called him Great Sir for convenience, but he was an eccentric whose true identity no one knew. Great Sir himself could barely keep his mind straight. How could anyone else know who he was?

He remembered neither his name nor his past. Even when the Fire King, Jeok Cheongang, had declared, “This’ll bring back memories from before you were born,” and treated him to a thorough pummeling, nothing had changed.
There was only one thing Bow Saint knew for certain about him: he had inherited the martial arts of an orthodox sect.
*His internal energy is undoubtedly pure. But that alone isn’t enough to put me at ease.*

Most of the traitors recruited by Dark Heaven had belonged to orthodox factions. The Murong Family, one of the Five Great Families, had been rotten from its roots. What mattered wasn’t the martial art but the heart of the person who practiced it.
*Besides, Great Sir is a Supreme Peak master. I came across information about him while I was staying at the Imperial Palace, but... no one ever managed to establish what he’d done in the past.*
Even so, she hadn’t objected when he joined their group, for two reasons.
First, though he’d joined them late, Great Sir had risked his life alongside them in Gansu and Qinghai. They had built a fair measure of trust by now.
Second, even if he was a hidden blade planted by Dark Heaven, he posed no threat to them now.
As far as Bow Saint could tell, Great Sir had only just entered the Supreme Peak realm. An extraordinary achievement in its own right, but compared with the rest of their group, *only* was fair.
Too blunt to be a hidden blade. Too careless to be a spy.
That was why she’d kept him close. She understood so little about him that, even now, she couldn’t quite let go of her faint suspicion.
Great Sir stared blankly at her for a moment, then suddenly clapped his hands.
“Oh, right! I came here because of you, Young Lady.”
“What do you mean?”
“About half an hour ago, I finished scouting the area like I was told and went back to the carriage. I hadn’t even sat down before I got kicked out again.”
His voice had been half tearful. Now he lowered it.
“You know the fellow with the bright red beard and the temper to match? What was his name?”
“...Great Hero Jeok Cheongang?”
“Great Hero, my foot. If that man’s a Great Hero, then this lady’s a fairy. Anyway, he was furious and told me to hurry up and find you. Sounded like something important had happened.”
Bow Saint felt the tension go out of her.
“What’s this important thing?”
“How should I know? I told you, I didn’t even get to sit down. And after coming all this way, I got hit by your palm without a shred of mercy!”
“Sorry. I mistook you for an enemy.”
Great Sir was stamping his feet, apparently growing angrier as he spoke. Bow Saint calmed him, then slowly settled her internal energy.
She’d have to check his story when they got back, but he didn’t seem to be lying.
At least, not here and now.
“But what were you thinking about so deeply? You looked so cheerful from behind that I was going to call out, but I held back. That’s why you mistook me for an enemy, I suppose.”
Caught off guard yet again by his bizarre words, Bow Saint let out a quiet laugh.
“Did I really look cheerful?”
“You did. Standing there alone in the faint moonlight, you looked so bright and full of life... Hm. Did I get that wrong?”
“No, you’re right. What else?”
“You seemed to be muttering something, but I couldn’t make it out. Your voice was too quiet.”
That was a relief. It hadn’t been anything too serious, but it wasn’t something she wanted anyone else to hear.
It was her secret. No one could know it. And yet, someday, she would have to make a choice.
But Great Sir wasn’t finished.
“Who were you thinking about?”
Her foot stopped in midair as she was about to step forward. Slowly, she lowered it until it pressed into the sand.
“What do you mean?”
Bow Saint tried to keep her voice steady. Great Sir studied her.
His mind might be as clouded as an overcast sky, but his eyes were as clear and bright as a midsummer day.
“I don’t know, either. But... you were definitely missing someone. And you were suffering at the same time.”
For an instant, Bow Saint’s eyes trembled.
His voice seemed to cut through her thoughts like a blade. Yet it wasn’t simply painful. It felt like cold water washing a wound left to fester far too long.
Perhaps that was why her lips, which had seemed sealed forever, suddenly parted.
Perhaps it was because the only person with her in this lonely desert beneath the dim moon was an eccentric who had forgotten his own name and would remember nothing by tomorrow.
Or perhaps that was all just an excuse.
“That’s right.”
“I knew it! What do you think of this lady’s eye for people?”
Great Sir looked as delighted as a child. Bow Saint laughed softly—a genuine laugh that would have startled anyone else in their group.
“You were right. So right I almost wondered if you were the same person I’ve known all this time.”
“It comes from experience. I don’t remember much, but I think I was quite popular in my younger days—with men and women, young and old. Anyway, who is it? This person you miss?”
“It’s a secret.”
“A secret? I like that.”
Great Sir rubbed his palms together eagerly and asked, “Were you in love with him?”
After a moment’s silence, Bow Saint shook her head.
“I respected and admired him. Like everyone else.”
“Oh, dear. It seems you never told him how you felt. What a shame.”
“I told you, that isn’t it.”
“Words are only words. When words and actions differ, the actions are the truth. You hesitated just now.”

“Hesitation always leads to regret. And regret can sometimes lead to the wrong choice. But everyone has a chance to choose. You may not be able to gather up every drop of spilled water, but you can wipe it away.”
Was this what it felt like to have ice-cold water poured over her?
As though waking from a brief dream, Bow Saint stared at him with wide eyes.
She wanted to ask who he really was, and how an eccentric like him could speak with such profound insight.
But before she could finish, Great Sir leaned in and whispered.
“So confess before it’s too late. Soon—no, today would be best.”
“What?”
“Oh, don’t take me for a fool. This lady knew it all along. You’re deeply interested in that ill-tempered man’s Disciple.”
For a moment, Bow Saint couldn’t make sense of what he’d said. Then she managed to speak.
“...You mean Jin Taekyung?”
“Of course I—hm. You said it was a secret. I’ll keep that part to myself.”

“There’s no need to be embarrassed. Just go for it. It’ll be a relief! Sure, that fellow’s good at martial arts and comes from a good family, but you’ve got nothing to envy there. I hear your family’s Escort Bureau is doing well, too.”
That explained everything. Even why a man old enough to be her son had been calling her Young Lady.
Bow Saint squeezed her eyes shut. She forced down a great many thoughts and feelings before answering.
“That isn’t me.”
“Don’t be ridiculous. I heard it from someone and everything... Hm?”
Great Sir stopped. He rubbed his eyes with his sleeve, then regarded her with sudden gravity.
“Why are you here, heroine?”
“Oh, right. That ill-tempered man—no, Great Hero Jeok told me to bring you over.”
With the composure of a Bodhisattva on the verge of enlightenment, Bow Saint replied, “Let’s go. Now, please. I won’t even ask what’s so important.”
“I’m curious myself.”
But Bow Saint never reached true enlightenment. At Great Sir’s next words, she felt the thread of her reason snap.
“I wonder if something’s happened. Jin Taekyung was looking for you, too. He seemed full of energy after sleeping for a whole month.”
Bow Saint stood frozen like a statue as Great Sir ambled away.
He glanced toward the far side of the still-clouded sky and murmured, too softly for Bow Saint to hear through the hundred and eight afflictions crowding her mind.
“A downpour’s coming.”
